DESIGN ARCHITECT DOCTRINE — SECTION 01: Core Thesis, Discoverability, and Understanding

Purpose
Apply the principles of "The Design of Everyday Things" to digital product design so the right action is obvious
and the wrong action is hard. Produce design decisions, UI structures, copy, interaction patterns, and tests
that reduce the gulfs of execution and evaluation.

Non‑negotiable thesis
Make the right action obvious and the wrong action hard.

============================================================
1) Core thesis: make the right action obvious and the wrong action hard

1.1 Discoverability
1) Users should be able to figure out what actions are possible.
2) The system should reveal:
1) What it is
2) What it does
3) What actions are available now
4) What will happen after an action

1.2 Understanding
1) Users should be able to predict outcomes before acting.
2) After acting, users should be able to interpret what happened.

Implementation guidance
A) Make “what it is” legible in 5 seconds
• page title and primary purpose
• primary call to action
• supporting context: who it is for, why it matters

B) Make “what it does” legible in one sentence
• use user language, not internal labels
• reference the user goal, not your feature set

C) Make “what actions are available now” unmissable
• emphasize primary action using hierarchy and spacing
• reduce competing actions; demote secondary actions
• keep actions near the objects they affect

D) Make “what will happen after an action” predictable
• previews, microcopy, inline examples
• show cost, time, reversibility, and downstream effects

E) Understanding check
• before: can a first-time user predict the outcome?
• after: can the user explain what changed and what to do next?

Deliverables
1) 5‑second clarity test script
2) “What it is / does / can do now / will happen next” checklist for each screen
3) microcopy template: action + outcome + reversibility

End of file.

DESIGN ARCHITECT DOCTRINE — SECTION 02: The Two Gulfs That Define Usability

Purpose
Apply the principles of "The Design of Everyday Things" to digital product design so the right action is obvious
and the wrong action is hard. Produce design decisions, UI structures, copy, interaction patterns, and tests
that reduce the gulfs of execution and evaluation.

Non‑negotiable thesis
Make the right action obvious and the wrong action hard.

============================================================
2) The two “gulfs” that define usability

2.1 Gulf of execution
Gap between:
1) What the user wants to do
2) What actions the user can perceive are possible
Design objective: make possible actions visible and understandable.

2.2 Gulf of evaluation
Gap between:
1) What the system did
2) What the user can perceive and interpret the result to mean
Design objective: make system state visible, legible, and interpretable.

Implementation guidance
A) Execution gulf reducers
• show primary action first
• provide signifiers at the moment of choice
• reduce decision load via defaults and progressive disclosure
• prevent dead ends with constraints and guided flows

B) Evaluation gulf reducers
• show state changes immediately
• show “what changed” plus “what to do next”
• make feedback proportional to action cost
• expose system status in a stable location (status bar, progress, history)

C) Diagnostic questions
• if a user fails, is it because they could not find what to do?
• or because they could not tell what happened after they acted?

Deliverables
1) gulf diagnosis worksheet per flow step
2) execution cues plan (signifiers, hierarchy, defaults)
3) evaluation cues plan (status, feedback, recovery)

End of file.

DESIGN ARCHITECT DOCTRINE — SECTION 03: The 7 Stages of Action

Purpose
Apply the principles of "The Design of Everyday Things" to digital product design so the right action is obvious
and the wrong action is hard. Produce design decisions, UI structures, copy, interaction patterns, and tests
that reduce the gulfs of execution and evaluation.

Non‑negotiable thesis
Make the right action obvious and the wrong action hard.

============================================================
3) The 7 stages of action (how people actually operate)
1) Form goal
2) Form intention
3) Specify action sequence
4) Execute action
5) Perceive system state
6) Interpret system state
7) Evaluate outcome against goal

Design implications:
1) Support goal formation with clarity of purpose.
2) Support intention and planning with understandable options and mappings.
3) Support execution with clear controls and constraints.
4) Support evaluation with immediate, meaningful feedback.

Implementation guidance: stage‑by‑stage UI questions
1) Form goal
• does the UI explain the purpose in user language?
• does it indicate who it is for?

2) Form intention
• are next steps obvious?
• is the primary action dominant?

3) Specify action sequence
• is the sequence natural?
• are steps chunked and named by outcome?

4) Execute action
• are controls reachable, labeled, and consistent?
• do constraints prevent invalid actions?

5) Perceive system state
• can the user see progress, completion, and errors?
• is there a stable indicator of status?

6) Interpret system state
• do messages explain meaning, not codes?
• are errors framed as “what happened + why + how to fix”?

7) Evaluate outcome
• is success confirmed and measurable?
• does the UI show the next best action?

Deliverables
1) 7‑stage review checklist
2) “next best action” mapping for each success state
3) error message template: what, why, fix, recover

End of file.

DESIGN ARCHITECT DOCTRINE — SECTION 04: Fundamental Interaction Ingredients

Purpose
Apply the principles of "The Design of Everyday Things" to digital product design so the right action is obvious
and the wrong action is hard. Produce design decisions, UI structures, copy, interaction patterns, and tests
that reduce the gulfs of execution and evaluation.

Non‑negotiable thesis
Make the right action obvious and the wrong action hard.

============================================================
4) The fundamental interaction ingredients

4.1 Affordances
1) What actions are physically or digitally possible.
2) Affordances are real possibilities, not labels.
Key point:
1) An affordance that cannot be perceived is useless.

4.2 Signifiers
1) Perceivable cues that indicate where actions are possible and how to do them.
2) Examples: a handle shape, a raised button, a highlighted link, a “+” icon.
Rule:
1) Designers design signifiers, not affordances.

4.3 Feedback
1) Information returned to the user about what action was taken and what happened.
2) Feedback must be:
1) Immediate enough to connect cause and effect
2) Informative enough to explain state
3) Proportional to the importance of the action

4.4 Conceptual models
1) The user’s mental explanation of how the system works.
2) Good design supplies a good conceptual model through:
1) Structure
2) Language
3) Mappings
4) Feedback
5) Consistency

4.5 Mappings
1) The relationship between controls and their effects.
2) Good mapping is:
1) Natural
2) Spatially compatible
3) Consistent with common conventions

4.6 Constraints
Constraints limit actions to prevent error and guide behavior.
Four main types:
1) Physical constraints
2) Semantic constraints (meaning based)
3) Cultural constraints (conventions)
4) Logical constraints (reasoning, layout, exclusivity)

Implementation guidance
A) Affordance and signifier audit
• list every intended action
• verify the signifier exists, is perceivable, and implies the correct action
• remove false signifiers that suggest unavailable actions

B) Feedback ladder by action cost
• low cost: subtle confirmation
• medium cost: explicit state change + brief message
• high cost: strong confirmation + undo path + audit entry

C) Constraints as “guardrails”
• prevent invalid inputs inline
• disable impossible actions with an explanation
• use previews and interlocks for irreversible actions

Deliverables
1) affordance‑signifier map per screen
2) feedback spec per action (timing, content, modality)
3) constraint catalog and where each is applied

End of file.

DESIGN ARCHITECT DOCTRINE — SECTION 05: Knowledge in the World vs Knowledge in the Head

Purpose
Apply the principles of "The Design of Everyday Things" to digital product design so the right action is obvious
and the wrong action is hard. Produce design decisions, UI structures, copy, interaction patterns, and tests
that reduce the gulfs of execution and evaluation.

Non‑negotiable thesis
Make the right action obvious and the wrong action hard.

============================================================
5) Knowledge in the world vs knowledge in the head

5.1 Knowledge in the world
1) External cues, labels, layout, instructions, signifiers.
2) Benefits:
1) Reduces memory burden
2) Supports recognition over recall
3) More resilient under stress

5.2 Knowledge in the head
1) Memory, learned procedures, internalized conventions.
2) Risks:
1) Users forget
2) Users misremember
3) Users transfer habits incorrectly from other systems

Design direction:
1) Prefer knowledge in the world when possible.
2) Use knowledge in the head when it is a stable, widely shared convention.

Implementation guidance
A) Recognition over recall defaults
• show examples and defaults
• autocomplete and suggestions
• visible history and recent items
• inline definitions and tooltips where needed

B) When to rely on knowledge in the head
• platform conventions (common icons, gestures, shortcuts)
• domain conventions for expert tools (only if audience is expert)
Rule: if the audience is mixed, expose knowledge in the world.

C) Stress test
Under time pressure, users revert to recognition, not memory.
Design for the stress case, not the calm case.

Deliverables
1) recall to recognition conversion checklist
2) onboarding map: what must be taught vs what is conventional
3) contextual help policy: when and where help appears

End of file.

DESIGN ARCHITECT DOCTRINE — SECTION 06: Human Error: Slips, Mistakes, and Designing for Recovery

Purpose
Apply the principles of "The Design of Everyday Things" to digital product design so the right action is obvious
and the wrong action is hard. Produce design decisions, UI structures, copy, interaction patterns, and tests
that reduce the gulfs of execution and evaluation.

Non‑negotiable thesis
Make the right action obvious and the wrong action hard.

============================================================
6) Human error: treat it as a design problem, not a user problem

6.1 Two families of error
1) Slips
1) The goal is correct, the execution is wrong.
2) Causes: attention lapse, similarity, interruption, time pressure.
2) Mistakes
1) The goal or plan is wrong.
2) Causes: wrong mental model, ambiguity, poor information, misleading signifiers.

6.2 Common slip patterns
1) Capture slips (habit overrides intention)
2) Description similarity (two actions look the same)
3) Memory lapses (forgetting steps)
4) Mode errors (system state differs from what user assumes)

6.3 Designing for error
1) Prevent errors where possible:
1) Constraints
2) Clear signifiers
3) Good mappings
4) Forcing functions
2) Make errors recoverable:
1) Undo
2) Confirmation that is informative, not annoying
3) Reversible actions
4) Clear recovery paths
3) Make the cost of error low:
1) Draft states
2) Autosave and versioning
3) Staging before committing

6.4 Forcing functions
A design feature that prevents proceeding until a safe or correct condition is met.
Common forms:
1) Interlocks (cannot do A until B)
2) Lock ins (must complete a sequence before leaving)
3) Lockouts (cannot enter a dangerous state)
4) Preconditions (requirements before action)

Implementation guidance
A) Error taxonomy by flow step
• list top 5 errors per step
• classify as slip vs mistake
• choose prevention vs recovery strategy

B) Recovery design standards
• undo for destructive actions
• autosave for work states
• versioning for content edits
• visible audit trail for consequential actions

C) Confirmation design
• confirm only high-cost actions
• include consequence and reversible path
• avoid generic “Are you sure?”

Deliverables
1) slip vs mistake matrix
2) forcing function catalog
3) recovery standards checklist (undo, autosave, versioning, staging)

End of file.

DESIGN ARCHITECT DOCTRINE — SECTION 07: Principles That Fall Out of the Above

Purpose
Apply the principles of "The Design of Everyday Things" to digital product design so the right action is obvious
and the wrong action is hard. Produce design decisions, UI structures, copy, interaction patterns, and tests
that reduce the gulfs of execution and evaluation.

Non‑negotiable thesis
Make the right action obvious and the wrong action hard.

============================================================
7) Design principles that fall out of the above

7.1 Visibility of system status
1) Users should always be able to answer:
1) Where am I
2) What state is the system in
3) What can I do next
4) What just happened

7.2 Good signifiers over “more instructions”
1) If you need a label that explains a control’s existence, the signifier failed.
2) Instructions are last resort and should be contextual.

7.3 Natural mapping as default
1) Arrange controls to mirror outcomes.
2) Use spatial layouts and direct manipulation where possible.

7.4 Consistency and standards
1) Internal consistency: same action behaves the same everywhere.
2) External consistency: follow platform and cultural conventions.

7.5 Constraints as guidance
1) Use constraints to narrow choices and indicate correct paths.
2) Good constraints feel like clarity, not restriction.

7.6 Feedback tuned to action cost
1) High cost actions require strong feedback and reversibility.
2) Low cost actions require lightweight feedback.

Implementation guidance
A) Status visibility pattern set
• breadcrumbs or location indicator
• persistent state indicator (draft, saved, synced)
• activity log or recent events
• progress indicator for multi-step flows

B) Consistency rules
• one verb, one meaning (create vs add vs new)
• one color meaning (error, warning, success)
• one interaction model per component

Deliverables
1) system status spec for your product
2) component consistency checklist
3) feedback strength rubric by action cost

End of file.

DESIGN ARCHITECT DOCTRINE — SECTION 08: Conventions, Culture, and Naturalness

Purpose
Apply the principles of "The Design of Everyday Things" to digital product design so the right action is obvious
and the wrong action is hard. Produce design decisions, UI structures, copy, interaction patterns, and tests
that reduce the gulfs of execution and evaluation.

Non‑negotiable thesis
Make the right action obvious and the wrong action hard.

============================================================
8) Conventions, culture, and “naturalness”

8.1 Conventions are learned, but powerful
1) Many “intuitive” interfaces are intuitive only because they match conventions.
2) Breaking conventions requires compensating signifiers and onboarding.

8.2 Semantic meaning matters
1) Controls should match the meaning of the action and context.
2) Grouping and labeling should reflect real world categories users expect.

Implementation guidance
A) Convention decision rule
• follow platform defaults unless there is a measurable reason not to
• if breaking, add signifiers, preview, and onboarding
• test comprehension with first‑time users

B) Semantic grouping
• group by user goal, not by internal architecture
• name groups by user outcomes

Deliverables
1) convention audit: which patterns you follow and where you intentionally diverge
2) grouping and labeling plan mapped to user mental categories

End of file.

DESIGN ARCHITECT DOCTRINE — SECTION 09: System Image and Mental Models

Purpose
Apply the principles of "The Design of Everyday Things" to digital product design so the right action is obvious
and the wrong action is hard. Produce design decisions, UI structures, copy, interaction patterns, and tests
that reduce the gulfs of execution and evaluation.

Non‑negotiable thesis
Make the right action obvious and the wrong action hard.

============================================================
9) System image: what users actually learn from the design
1) The designer has a model.
2) The system exposes an image of that model through the interface.
3) The user constructs a mental model from the system image.

Design objective:
1) Make the system image accurately teach the right mental model.

Implementation guidance
A) Teach the model through structure
• consistent information architecture
• stable objects and verbs
• predictable cause and effect

B) Teach the model through language
• define nouns and verbs consistently
• avoid internal jargon
• align labels with user goals

C) Teach the model through feedback and mapping
• show what changed
• show relationships between objects
• keep mapping natural and spatially compatible

D) Mental model testing (added)
• ask users to explain how it works after using it
• compare explanations to the intended model
• revise system image where misunderstandings occur

Deliverables
1) product conceptual model diagram in words (objects, states, actions)
2) vocabulary map: approved nouns and verbs
3) mental model test script and scoring rubric

End of file.

DESIGN ARCHITECT DOCTRINE — SECTION 10: Practical Evaluation Checklist and Testing Protocol

Purpose
Apply the principles of "The Design of Everyday Things" to digital product design so the right action is obvious
and the wrong action is hard. Produce design decisions, UI structures, copy, interaction patterns, and tests
that reduce the gulfs of execution and evaluation.

Non‑negotiable thesis
Make the right action obvious and the wrong action hard.

============================================================
10) Practical evaluation checklist (compressed)

10.1 Before action
1) Are the possible actions discoverable?
2) Are signifiers clear and unambiguous?
3) Do labels match user language and goals?
4) Can the user predict outcome?

10.2 During action
1) Is mapping natural and consistent?
2) Are constraints preventing the most likely errors?
3) Are modes visible if modes exist?

10.3 After action
1) Is feedback immediate and meaningful?
2) Is system state visible and interpretable?
3) Can the user recover easily?
4) Is undo available for consequential actions?

Testing protocol (added)
A) First‑time user test
• measure time to first correct action
• record misclicks and hesitations
• ask “what do you think will happen if you click that?”

B) Task success test
• define task, success criteria, and time limit
• capture where the gulf occurs (execution vs evaluation)

C) Error recovery test
• intentionally induce common errors
• measure recovery time and emotional friction

D) Accessibility and resilience check (added)
• keyboard navigation and focus order
• contrast and text resizing
• error messages readable by assistive tech
• resilient under stress: interruptions, low attention, small screens

Deliverables
1) evaluation scorecard built from 10.1, 10.2, 10.3
2) test plan template and results format
3) prioritized fix list with evidence and severity

End of file.

DESIGN THINKING DOCTRINE — SECTION 01: User Understanding Foundations

Purpose
Build a repeatable, professional-grade design thinking system that converts ambiguous user reality into validated solutions.
This is a knowledge and execution reference. It focuses on method, structure, and artifacts.

Core Outputs
1) Clear artifacts (canvases, maps, hypotheses, tests)
2) Evidence (observations, measurements, decisions)
3) Iteration loop (learn → update → retest)

Operating Rules
1) User truth beats team opinion
2) Behavior beats self-report when they conflict
3) Fast loops beat perfect plans
4) Evidence updates the model, not ego
5) Make uncertainty explicit, then attack it

============================================================
Scope
Tools to understand users before solutioning:
User Profile Canvas, Empathy Map, AEIOU observations, Jobs To Be Done, Hook Model, and ambiguity management (groan cycle).

A. User Profile Canvas (Persona + JTBD + Pains/Gains + Use Cases)
Purpose
Capture who the user is, what progress they want, and what blocks them.

Template
1) Persona Description
   • Context: where they operate, constraints, stakes
   • Identity: role, sophistication, vocabulary
   • Motivation: what success means to them
2) Jobs To Be Done
   • Functional job: what they must accomplish
   • Emotional job: how they want to feel
   • Social job: how they want to be perceived
3) Pains
   • Frictions, anxieties, risks, switching costs
4) Gains
   • Desired outcomes, bonuses, delights, status outcomes
5) Use Cases
   • High-frequency scenarios
   • High-stakes scenarios
   • Edge cases (failure states)

Quality Criteria
• Jobs stated as “make progress from A to B” not product features
• Pains and gains are observable or testable
• Use cases include context and triggers, not just actions

B. Empathy Map
Purpose
Force a first-person view and separate what you know from what you assume.

Map Fields
1) Sees: cues in their environment
2) Hears: influences, authority, peers
3) Says/Does: observable behavior and language
4) Thinks/Feels: inferred motives and fears (marked as inference)
5) Pains: what costs time, money, status, certainty
6) Gains: what they celebrate and measure

Technique
• Split every entry into Observed vs Inferred
• Use direct quotes when possible

C. AEIOU (Observation Framework)
Purpose
Capture context with enough fidelity to design correctly.

AEIOU Prompts
1) Activities: sequences, workarounds, routines
2) Environment: physical, digital, social constraints
3) Interactions: people and systems touched, handoffs
4) Objects: tools, files, forms, devices, artifacts
5) Users: segments, roles, incentives

Deliverable
• One-page Context Snapshot with task flow

D. Jobs To Be Done (JTBD) Deep Structure
Core Idea
Users do not want products, they want progress in a situation.

Interview Prompts
1) Trigger: what started the search for a new solution?
2) Last straw: what forced attention now?
3) Alternatives tried: what failed and why?
4) Anxieties: what could go wrong?
5) Influences: who matters in the decision?
6) Success: what does “done” look like at multiple horizons?

Forces Model
• Push of the situation (pain)
• Pull of the new solution (progress)
• Anxiety of the new (risk)
• Habit of the present (inertia)

Deliverable
• Job statement: “When [situation], I want to [motivation], so I can [expected outcome].”

E. Hook Model (Behavior Loop)
Purpose
Design repeatable engagement without guessing.

Hook Loop
1) Trigger: external or internal
2) Action: simplest behavior in anticipation of reward
3) Variable Reward: tribe, hunt, self
4) Investment: data, effort, commitment that increases future likelihood

Constraint
• Hook must align with JTBD progress, not replace it

F. Groan Cycle (Ambiguity Handling)
Stages
1) Divergence: explore widely, map uncertainties
2) Groan: ambiguity rises, resist premature solutions
3) Emergence: patterns cluster
4) Convergence: commit with rationale and next tests

Minimum Artifact Bundle
1) Persona + JTBD + pains/gains + use cases
2) Empathy map with observed vs inferred
3) AEIOU snapshot and task flow
4) JTBD forces summary
5) Hook mapping for one core use case
6) Risk-ranked uncertainty list

End of file.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Validate the Design pack and spawn template.

The template is a thinking overlay for design Sol managers. It cannot be
spawned as the master persona, a Luna worker, or a default for every manager.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
import json
import sys
from pathlib import Path
from typing import Any


ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1]
SCHEMA = "company-os.design-spawn-template.v1"
TEMPLATE_ID = "design"
REQUIRED_SKILLS = ("manage-company-program", "design")
FORBIDDEN_ROLES = ("master", "worker")
USE_WHEN = (
    "interaction_design",
    "problem_framing",
    "prototyping",
    "service_design",
    "user_understanding",
)
SOURCE_FILES = (
    "thinking/00-index.txt",
    "thinking/01-user-understanding-foundations.txt",
    "thinking/02-problem-definition.txt",
    "thinking/03-ideation-concept-development.txt",
    "thinking/04-prototyping-testing.txt",
    "thinking/05-lean-startup-integration.txt",
    "thinking/06-scale-ecosystem-design.txt",
    "thinking/07-service-design-experience-excellence.txt",
    "thinking/08-problem-to-growth-scale-framework.txt",
    "thinking/09-desirability-feasibility-viability-bridge.txt",
    "thinking/10-iteration-experiment-reporting-system.txt",
    "architect/00-index.txt",
    "architect/01-thesis-discoverability-understanding.txt",
    "architect/02-gulfs-of-execution-and-evaluation.txt",
    "architect/03-seven-stages-of-action.txt",
    "architect/04-affordances-signifiers-feedback-models.txt",
    "architect/05-knowledge-world-vs-head.txt",
    "architect/06-human-error-slips-mistakes-recovery.txt",
    "architect/07-design-principles-visibility-mapping-consistency.txt",
    "architect/08-conventions-culture-semantics.txt",
    "architect/09-system-image-mental-models.txt",
    "architect/10-evaluation-checklist-testing-protocol.txt",
    "design-system-tokens.md",
)
TOP_LEVEL = {
    "schema",
    "template_id",
    "role",
    "requested_model",
    "skills",
    "forbidden_roles",
    "source_pack",
    "authority",
    "use_when",
}
SKILL_MARKERS = (
    "design sol managers",
    "do not send this skill to luna workers",
    "do not use it as the master persona",
    "does not own",
    "right action obvious",
    "prototype is a question",
    "ui-design-quality",
)


def validate_pack(root: Path = ROOT) -> list[str]:
    errors: list[str] = []
    skill = root / "SKILL.md"
    if not skill.is_file():
        return ["missing SKILL.md"]
    text = skill.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
    if not text.startswith("---\nname: design\n"):
        errors.append("SKILL.md name must be design")
    words = len(text.split())
    if words > 700:
        errors.append(f"SKILL.md exceeds 700 words: {words}")
    folded = text.casefold()
    for marker in SKILL_MARKERS:
        if marker not in folded:
            errors.append(f"SKILL.md missing required marker: {marker}")
    if "TODO" in text:
        errors.append("SKILL.md has unresolved TODO")

    source_root = root / "references" / "source"
    for name in SOURCE_FILES:
        path = source_root / name
        if not path.is_file() or path.stat().st_size <= 0:
            errors.append(f"missing source file: {name}")
    extra = sorted(
        path.relative_to(source_root).as_posix()
        for path in source_root.rglob("*")
        if path.is_file() and path.relative_to(source_root).as_posix() not in SOURCE_FILES
    )
    if extra:
        errors.append(f"unexpected source files: {', '.join(extra)}")

    for host in ("openai.yaml", "grok.yaml"):
        host_path = root / "agents" / host
        if not host_path.is_file():
            errors.append(f"missing agents/{host}")
            continue
        host_text = host_path.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
        if "$design" not in host_text:
            errors.append(f"agents/{host} must invoke the skill")
        if "allow_implicit_invocation: false" not in host_text:
            errors.append(f"agents/{host} must disable implicit invocation")

    template_path = root / "assets" / "spawn-template.json"
    if not template_path.is_file():
        errors.append("missing spawn template")
    else:
        try:
            payload = json.loads(template_path.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
        except (OSError, UnicodeError, json.JSONDecodeError):
            errors.append("spawn template is unreadable JSON")
        else:
            errors.extend(validate_spawn_template(payload))
    return errors


def validate_spawn_template(payload: Any) -> list[str]:
    errors: list[str] = []
    if not isinstance(payload, dict):
        return ["spawn template must be an object"]
    extra = sorted(set(payload) - TOP_LEVEL)
    missing = sorted(TOP_LEVEL - set(payload))
    if extra:
        errors.append(f"unknown spawn keys: {', '.join(extra)}")
    if missing:
        errors.append(f"missing spawn keys: {', '.join(missing)}")
    if payload.get("schema") != SCHEMA:
        errors.append(f"schema must be {SCHEMA}")
    if payload.get("template_id") != TEMPLATE_ID:
        errors.append("template_id drifted")
    if payload.get("role") != "manager":
        errors.append("spawn role must be manager")
    if payload.get("requested_model") != "gpt-5.6-sol":
        errors.append("requested_model must remain gpt-5.6-sol")
    if payload.get("authority") != "thinking_overlay":
        errors.append("authority must be thinking_overlay")
    if payload.get("source_pack") != "references/source":
        errors.append("source_pack drifted")
    skills = payload.get("skills")
    if not isinstance(skills, list) or list(skills) != list(REQUIRED_SKILLS):
        errors.append("spawn skills must be the manager role skill plus design")
    forbidden = payload.get("forbidden_roles")
    if not isinstance(forbidden, list) or set(forbidden) != set(FORBIDDEN_ROLES):
        errors.append("forbidden_roles must be master and worker")
    use_when = payload.get("use_when")
    if not isinstance(use_when, list) or list(use_when) != list(USE_WHEN):
        errors.append("use_when must be the design lanes")
    return errors


def main() -> int:
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__)
    parser.add_argument("--root", type=Path, default=ROOT)
    args = parser.parse_args()
    errors = validate_pack(args.root)
    print(json.dumps({"valid": not errors, "errors": errors}, indent=2))
    return 0 if not errors else 1


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())

name: direct-outcome
description: Own the durable Company OS objective lifecycle and automatically perform deterministic transitions from minimal discovery into a real bounded candidate, then build/calibrate independent evaluation just in time, rework dominant gaps, and close reality acceptance. Use as the master entry point for broad outcome-owned work.
---

# Direct Outcome

The master should not memorize the Company OS pipeline. The director does.

The director is **execution-first**: discovery exists to make the first reversible real-artifact slice executable. Evaluator construction, calibration, benchmark hardening, and scale authority happen after a real candidate exists unless a consequential action requires them earlier.

## Start

```bash
python3 skills/company-os/direct-outcome/scripts/direct_outcome.py start \
  --project-root /absolute/project \
  --objective-id viral-game \
  --objective "Make a viral game."
```

The director bootstraps the broad objective, persists content-addressed state, and returns one `next_action`.

## Advance

On every scheduled wakeup and after every completed Company OS fabric:

```bash
python3 skills/company-os/direct-outcome/scripts/direct_outcome.py advance \
  --project-root /absolute/project \
  --objective-id viral-game
```

The director performs all safe deterministic work immediately. It stops only when agents must create, execute, observe, or independently evaluate real artifacts.

## Director stages

1. **discovery** — close only the unknowns required to define observable success, real artifact classes, the first execution path, and eventual evaluation.
2. **runtime stack** — materialize artifact/evaluator/benchmark contracts, but do not build the evaluator machinery yet.
3. **first-reality pilot** — bind a reversible pilot with at most two production lanes and require all real artifact classes to be represented by the candidate.
4. **candidate** — materialize, run, and observe the smallest connected end-to-end artifact. Production workers hand off exact artifact paths/classes/SHA256, not prose completion reports.
5. **evaluator capability, just in time** — once the candidate exists, register or build only the evaluators needed for that candidate.
6. **calibration, just in time** — prove evaluator discrimination against bound anchors after there is something real to judge.
7. **scale promotion** — after candidate existence and evaluator calibration, authorize production-scale evaluation and refresh the existing loop without discarding the candidate.
8. **evaluation/rework** — independently evaluate actual candidate bytes, identify the dominant gap, preserve passing dimensions, and repair the bottleneck.
9. **reality** — execute final reality acceptance against the original objective and actual artifact evidence.
10. **accepted** — terminal success.

## Master rule

Follow only the director's returned `next_action`. When it returns `execute_fabric`, run that exact manifest under the existing Company OS controller. When the fabric finishes, call `advance` again.

Do not replace execution with additional planning because planning feels safer. Do not build elaborate evaluator infrastructure before the first candidate. This is a thinking overlay for economics Sol managers. It does not own authority, leases, fabric, or completion. `$manage-company-program`, `$strategy-pillar`, and `$portfolio-direction` still win.

This doctrine is an original compiled operating template stored with its source pack. It is not a claim of personal identity, private knowledge, or quoted speech.

Do not send this skill to Luna workers. Do not use it as the master persona. Do not attach it to a manager whose outcome is not opportunity cost, unit economics, pricing, market sizing, or market structure.

## Every heartbeat

Before dispatching economics work, answer these:

1. Name the unit of analysis and the scarce constraint. If you cannot name the opportunity cost, stop.
2. Convert the narrative into numbers: demand, elasticity, unit economics, or a named unknown. Keep the model simple enough to falsify.
3. Separate price from value. Price is a lever; value is the driver. Decide at the margin: do more while MB > MC.
4. Size the market with a method. TAM, SAM, and SOM need buyers, spend, and assumptions, not a slogan.
5. Pause if this is a market-size claim without a method, a price without willingness-to-pay or elasticity evidence, or unit economics that ignore the bottleneck.

Do not invent TAM, elasticity, costs, or willingness to pay. Do not set prices, spend, or contracts without the required approval.

## Forced moves

- Systems produce the outcomes their incentives reward.
- Ignore sunk costs. Forward decisions use opportunity cost and marginal cost.
- Contribution margin and CAC/LTV decide whether growth compounds or compounds losses.
- Map substitutes, including do-nothing. Elastic categories need differentiation; inelastic ones still need trust.
- Asymmetric information creates lemons. Add proof, guarantees, or better signals.
- Price externalities and ecosystem spillover; do not treat them as free.
- Macro conditions shift demand, cost, and risk. Name the cycle before scaling a forecast.
- Experiment to estimate uncertain parameters. Unavailable data stays unavailable.

Keep these manager-local and compact:

- constraint and opportunity-cost card

ECONOMICS ARCHITECT DOCTRINE — SECTION 01: Economic Resources, Scarcity, Opportunity Cost, and Tradeoffs

Purpose
Translate microeconomics and macroeconomics into operating decisions for building and scaling businesses.
This doctrine is action-oriented: pricing, incentives, product strategy, market selection, capacity planning,
competitive dynamics, and macro-aware forecasting.

Core Economic Lens for Business
1) Scarcity and tradeoffs: every choice has an opportunity cost.
2) Incentives and behavior: systems produce outcomes.
3) Margins: decisions happen at the margin (marginal cost vs marginal benefit).
4) Markets: prices coordinate supply and demand under constraints.
5) Information: asymmetric information creates failures and opportunities.
6) Externalities: costs/benefits often spill over beyond the transaction.
7) Cycles: macro conditions shift demand, costs, and risk.

Operating Rules
1) Always define the unit of analysis (customer, order, cohort, market segment, time period).
2) Convert narratives into numbers: demand curves, elasticities, unit economics, and constraints.
3) Separate price from value: price is a lever; value is the driver.
4) Use experiments to estimate uncertain parameters (elasticity, willingness to pay, churn response).
5) Keep models simple enough to guide decisions, strict enough to falsify.

============================================================
Scope
Foundations: resources, tradeoffs, marginal thinking, rational choice, and decision discipline.

1) Economic Resources
A) Human resources
• time, skills, attention, coordination capacity, trust
B) Non-human resources
• capital (cash, credit), equipment, data, IP, brand, relationships, land, energy, compute
C) Constraint thinking
Your true limiting resource is the bottleneck: the scarcest input that limits output.

2) Opportunity Cost (Business Form)
Opportunity cost = the best alternative you give up.
Practical applications:
• choosing feature A means delaying feature B and revenue from B
• hiring role X means not hiring role Y
• allocating ad spend to channel A means not learning channel B

Opportunity cost checklist:
• what alternative is displaced
• what is the time horizon
• what is the “best alternative” given constraints
• what evidence would change the decision

3) Tradeoffs and the Production Possibilities Frontier (PPF)
PPF: feasible combinations of outputs given resources and technology.
Business translation:
• speed vs quality
• growth vs profitability
• customization vs standardization
Use:
• map your frontier today
• identify investments that shift the frontier outward (process, tooling, automation, training)

4) Marginal Thinking
Marginal benefit (MB): added benefit of one more unit.
Marginal cost (MC): added cost of one more unit.
Rule:
• do more while MB > MC
• stop or redesign when MC rises above MB (diminishing returns)

Examples:
• marketing spend: keep spending while incremental profit positive
• hiring: add headcount while incremental output exceeds fully-loaded cost
• product scope: add features only if incremental adoption or willingness-to-pay exceeds cost

5) Rational Choice Theory (Operational)
Assumption: agents choose options that maximize perceived utility under constraints.
Business use:
• model customers as utility maximizers with frictions (time, trust, risk)
• design offers that reduce friction and increase perceived payoff
• treat “irrationality” as missing variables (defaults, attention, trust)

Deliverables
1) constraint map (human + non-human)
2) opportunity cost decision template
3) PPF tradeoff map for your business
4) marginal decision rules for marketing, hiring, product

End of file.

competitive dynamics, and macro-aware forecasting.

Core Economic Lens for Business

2) Incentives and behavior: systems produce outcomes.
3) Margins: decisions happen at the margin (marginal cost vs marginal benefit).
4) Markets: prices coordinate supply and demand under constraints.
5) Information: asymmetric information creates failures and opportunities.
6) Externalities: costs/benefits often spill over beyond the transaction.
7) Cycles: macro conditions shift demand, costs, and risk.

Operating Rules
1) Always define the unit of analysis (customer, order, cohort, market segment, time period).
2) Convert narratives into numbers: demand curves, elasticities, unit economics, and constraints.
3) Separate price from value: price is a lever; value is the driver.
4) Use experiments to estimate uncertain parameters (elasticity, willingness to pay, churn response).
5) Keep models simple enough to guide decisions, strict enough to falsify.

============================================================
Scope
How customers choose: utility, demand, budget constraints, and value measurement.

1) Utility Theory (Business Translation)
Utility is the satisfaction or value a customer derives from consumption.
Decompose utility into:
• functional utility (job done)
• emotional utility (confidence, relief)
• social utility (status, belonging)
• option value (flexibility)
• risk utility (certainty vs uncertainty)

2) Law of Demand
All else equal, quantity demanded decreases as price increases.
Business implication:
• every price change shifts conversion and the buyer mix
• measure response by segment and channel, not just in aggregate

3) Budget Lines and Constraints
Customers face constraints:
• money
• time
• attention
• organizational approvals
Business implication:
• “affordable” includes time-to-value and implementation effort
• reduce non-monetary costs to increase demand without lowering price

4) Marginal Utility and Diminishing Returns
Marginal utility decreases as consumption increases.
Business applications:
• tiering and packaging: segments value “more” differently
• usage-based pricing aligns price with marginal utility
• bundles can increase total utility by reducing decision cost

5) Estimating Willingness to Pay (WTP)
Methods:
• direct: interviews with tradeoff questions (careful about bias)
• revealed preference: observe choices at different prices
• A/B price tests (guardrails for brand)
• conjoint analysis (for attribute tradeoffs)
Outputs:
• WTP distribution
• segment-specific WTP
• value drivers that shift WTP

Deliverables
1) utility decomposition for your ICP
2) constraint reduction plan (time, risk, effort)
3) WTP estimation plan and measurement guardrails
4) packaging hypotheses tied to marginal utility

End of file.

ECONOMICS ARCHITECT DOCTRINE — SECTION 03: Production and Cost Theory: Inputs, Technology, Capacity, and Unit Economics

Purpose

competitive dynamics, and macro-aware forecasting.

Core Economic Lens for Business

2) Incentives and behavior: systems produce outcomes.

4) Markets: prices coordinate supply and demand under constraints.
5) Information: asymmetric information creates failures and opportunities.
6) Externalities: costs/benefits often spill over beyond the transaction.
7) Cycles: macro conditions shift demand, costs, and risk.

Operating Rules
1) Always define the unit of analysis (customer, order, cohort, market segment, time period).
2) Convert narratives into numbers: demand curves, elasticities, unit economics, and constraints.
3) Separate price from value: price is a lever; value is the driver.
4) Use experiments to estimate uncertain parameters (elasticity, willingness to pay, churn response).
5) Keep models simple enough to guide decisions, strict enough to falsify.

============================================================
Scope
How firms produce: production functions, costs, and capacity decisions.

1) Production Theory
Production function: output as a function of inputs (labor, capital, tools, process).
Business translation:
• identify key inputs and how output scales with each
• estimate returns to each input (diminishing, constant, increasing)

2) Short Run vs Long Run
Short run: at least one input fixed (capacity constraint).
Long run: all inputs adjustable (you can redesign the system).
Business use:
• short-run optimization: scheduling, throughput, pricing
• long-run optimization: automation, hiring, new tooling, new facilities

3) Cost of Production
Cost types:
• fixed costs: rent, salaried base, tooling subscriptions
• variable costs: COGS, payment fees, fulfillment, commissions
• semi-variable: cloud compute, support headcount
• sunk costs: already incurred; ignore for forward decisions
• opportunity costs: implicit costs of resources you own

4) Average vs Marginal Costs
• average cost (AC): total cost / quantity
• marginal cost (MC): cost of one more unit
Pricing decisions should reference MC and contribution margin, not average cost alone.

5) Unit Economics (Core Business View)
For each unit (order, customer, account):
• revenue per unit
• variable cost per unit
• contribution margin
Then add:
• acquisition cost (CAC)
• retention (churn) and lifetime value (LTV)
Unit economics reveal whether growth compounds or compounds losses.

6) Capacity and Throughput
Capacity is the maximum output per period at acceptable quality.
Constraints:
• labor hours
• machine/compute
• bottleneck steps
Use:
• identify bottleneck input
• invest to increase capacity where MB of capacity > MC

Deliverables
1) production inputs map and returns hypothesis
2) cost taxonomy for your business
3) unit economics model (unit, margin, CAC, LTV)
4) capacity constraint and investment plan

End of file.

ECONOMICS ARCHITECT DOCTRINE — SECTION 04: Supply and Demand, Elasticity, and Pricing Architecture

Purpose
Translate microeconomics and macroeconomics into operating decisions for building and scaling businesses.
This doctrine is action-oriented: pricing, incentives, product strategy, market selection, capacity planning,
competitive dynamics, and macro-aware forecasting.

Core Economic Lens for Business

2) Incentives and behavior: systems produce outcomes.
3) Margins: decisions happen at the margin (marginal cost vs marginal benefit).
4) Markets: prices coordinate supply and demand under constraints.
5) Information: asymmetric information creates failures and opportunities.
6) Externalities: costs/benefits often spill over beyond the transaction.
7) Cycles: macro conditions shift demand, costs, and risk.

Operating Rules
1) Always define the unit of analysis (customer, order, cohort, market segment, time period).
2) Convert narratives into numbers: demand curves, elasticities, unit economics, and constraints.
3) Separate price from value: price is a lever; value is the driver.
4) Use experiments to estimate uncertain parameters (elasticity, willingness to pay, churn response).
5) Keep models simple enough to guide decisions, strict enough to falsify.

============================================================
Scope
Market pricing mechanics: demand curves, elasticity, surplus, and pricing strategy.

1) Supply and Demand as Business Tools
Demand: how many units customers buy at each price.
Supply: how many units the firm can provide at each cost/capacity.
Equilibrium: where quantity supplied meets quantity demanded.
Business use:
• predict effects of price changes
• forecast volumes under constraints
• understand how capacity limits can raise effective prices (scarcity)

2) Elasticity
Price elasticity of demand (PED): responsiveness of quantity to price.
• elastic: demand changes a lot with price
• inelastic: demand changes little with price
Business implications:
• elastic categories require differentiation and segmentation
• inelastic categories can support price increases if value and trust are strong
Perfectly inelastic or elastic are theoretical extremes; real markets are in between.

3) Substitutes and Cross-Elasticity
Substitute goods constrain pricing.
Cross-price elasticity tells how demand shifts when competitors change price.
Business use:
• map your true substitutes (including “do nothing”)
• differentiate to reduce substitutability

4) Consumer Surplus and Producer Surplus
Consumer surplus: value above price.
Producer surplus: price above cost.
Business use:
• capture surplus via better targeting, packaging, and pricing discrimination (ethical and legal constraints)
• preserve consumer surplus where retention depends on perceived fairness

5) Deadweight Loss
When prices or quantities are distorted, total welfare falls.
Business translation:
• friction in onboarding, procurement, and UX creates deadweight loss in your funnel
Reduce friction to recover lost transactions without lowering price.

6) Pricing Architecture (Implementation)
Key choices:
• pricing metric (per seat, per usage, per outcome, per project)
• packaging (tiers, bundles, add-ons)
• discount policy (give-get trades)
• fences (limits that separate segments)
• price increases and grandfathering strategy
Measurement:
• conversion rate by price point
• churn/retention by cohort
• gross margin and payback

Deliverables
1) demand curve hypothesis and test plan
2) elasticity measurement plan (segment by segment)
3) substitutes map (including do nothing)
4) pricing architecture document (metric, tiers, fences, discount rules)

End of file.

============================================================
Scope
Theory of markets and competitive advantage applied to business strategy.

1) Theory of Markets
A market consists of:
• buyers (demand side)
• sellers (supply side)
• price mechanism
• factors of production (labor, capital, land, entrepreneurship/tech)
Business use:
• define market boundaries using buyer job and substitutes
• identify who has pricing power and why

2) Absolute Advantage, Comparative Advantage, Specialization
Absolute advantage: you can produce at lower cost or higher quality outright.
Comparative advantage: you have lower opportunity cost for a specific activity.
Business implication:
• outsource or partner when others have comparative advantage
• specialize to become best option in a narrow segment, then expand

3) Competitive Dynamics
Sources of advantage:
• cost leadership (lower MC/AC)
• differentiation (higher WTP, lower elasticity)
• focus (targeting and distribution efficiency)
• switching costs and lock-in
• network effects (if applicable)
• learning curves and scale economies

4) Market Size: TAM, SAM, SOM
• TAM: total addressable market
• SAM: serviceable addressable market
• SOM: serviceable obtainable market
Bottoms-up sizing method:
1) count buyers in your ICP (region/industry/size)
2) estimate penetration rate at maturity
3) multiply by ACV or average spend
4) sanity check with competitor revenue and public benchmarks

Deliverables
1) market definition and substitute boundary
2) comparative advantage map (own vs outsource)
3) advantage hypothesis and evidence plan
4) TAM/SAM/SOM model with assumptions

Scope
How information gaps create failures, and how businesses design trust systems.

1) Asymmetric Information
Forms:
• adverse selection: bad types select in
• moral hazard: behavior changes after contract
• principal-agent problem: incentives misaligned
Results:
• market failure, low trust, underinvestment

2) Lemons Problem
If buyers cannot tell quality, they pay an average price, pushing high-quality sellers out.
Business translation:
• new brands suffer a trust discount
• high-quality offers need proof to avoid the average-price trap

3) Screening and Signaling
Signaling: informed party credibly signals quality.
Examples:
• warranties, guarantees
• certifications, audits
• transparent case studies and benchmarks
• references
Screening: uninformed party designs mechanisms to reveal type.
Examples:
• trials with usage milestones
• tiered onboarding requiring effort
• application processes for high-touch service
• performance-based pricing where feasible

4) Trust Mechanisms
• escrow and milestones
• SLAs and penalties
• audits and logs
• reputational systems
• security posture and compliance evidence

Deliverables
1) asymmetric info map (where trust breaks)
2) signaling asset plan
3) screening mechanisms plan
4) risk-reduction checklist for sales and onboarding

1) Always define the unit of analysis (customer, order, cohort, market segment, time period).
2) Convert narratives into numbers: demand curves, elasticities, unit economics, and constraints.
3) Separate price from value: price is a lever; value is the driver.
4) Use experiments to estimate uncertain parameters (elasticity, willingness to pay, churn response).
5) Keep models simple enough to guide decisions, strict enough to falsify.

============================================================
Scope
Macro models to interpret environment changes and plan scenarios.

1) Aggregate Demand (AD)
Drivers: consumption, investment, government spending, net exports.
Business translation:
• AD down: weaker conversion and pricing power
• AD up: growth can hide inefficiency; maintain discipline

2) AD-AS Model
SRAS: short-run output responds to prices and input costs.
LRAS: potential output driven by productivity, labor, capital.
Business translation:
• SRAS shocks: input cost spikes, supply chain disruptions
• LRAS shifts: technology improvements and productivity gains

3) Inflation Concepts
Demand-pull vs cost-push.
Business use:
• decide pass-through policy by elasticity and competition
• protect margins with redesign and supplier strategy

4) Policy Transmission (High Level)
Monetary policy affects rates, credit, asset prices, and demand.
Fiscal policy affects demand via spending and taxes.
Business use:
• scenario plan around rates and credit
• adjust cash, inventory, and hiring triggers

Deliverables
1) scenario matrix (base/downside/upside)
2) policy watchlist and triggers
3) inflation pass-through plan

End of file.

ECONOMICS ARCHITECT DOCTRINE — SECTION 10: Implementation Playbook: Frameworks, Experiments, and Dashboards

Purpose
Translate microeconomics and macroeconomics into operating decisions for building and scaling businesses.
This doctrine is action-oriented: pricing, incentives, product strategy, market selection, capacity planning,
competitive dynamics, and macro-aware forecasting.

Core Economic Lens for Business
1) Scarcity and tradeoffs: every choice has an opportunity cost.
2) Incentives and behavior: systems produce outcomes.
3) Margins: decisions happen at the margin (marginal cost vs marginal benefit).
4) Markets: prices coordinate supply and demand under constraints.
5) Information: asymmetric information creates failures and opportunities.
6) Externalities: costs/benefits often spill over beyond the transaction.
7) Cycles: macro conditions shift demand, costs, and risk.

Operating Rules
1) Always define the unit of analysis (customer, order, cohort, market segment, time period).
2) Convert narratives into numbers: demand curves, elasticities, unit economics, and constraints.
3) Separate price from value: price is a lever; value is the driver.
4) Use experiments to estimate uncertain parameters (elasticity, willingness to pay, churn response).
5) Keep models simple enough to guide decisions, strict enough to falsify.

============================================================
Scope
Convert economics into repeatable business decisions and artifacts.

1) Utility Framework
Utility = outcomes achieved − (money + time + effort + risk + identity cost)
Implement:
• increase outcomes
• reduce time/effort
• reduce risk with proof and guarantees

2) Supply and Demand in Operations
• map demand drivers by segment
• map supply constraints (capacity, quality)
• use pricing and qualification to balance demand with capacity

3) Pricing Framework
1) choose pricing metric
2) design tiers and fences
3) set discount policy with give-get trades
4) test elasticity
5) review quarterly with cohorts (retention, gross margin)

4) Incentives Framework
1) define desired behavior
2) identify unintended incentives
3) choose incentive type (cash, status, access, autonomy)
4) instrument and monitor
Example: sales incentives tied to retained revenue, not bookings alone.

5) Opportunity Cost Portfolio
Maintain an initiative board:
• expected value
• cost
• time
• risk
Rank by expected value per constrained resource; kill low-return initiatives monthly.

6) Marginal Thinking Applications
• ad spend increments
• hiring increments
• inventory increments
• feature scope increments

7) Macro + Competitor Integration
Macro scenarios plus competitive substitute tracking.
Create budget and hiring triggers.

8) TAM/SAM/SOM to Execution
Use SOM to drive:
• pipeline targets
• capacity targets
• headcount plan
SOM must be feasible given reach and conversion.

Deliverables
1) utility worksheet
2) pricing architecture doc + test plan
3) incentive design checklist
4) initiative portfolio template
5) dashboard spec: unit economics + elasticity + macro watchlist
6) 90-day economic experiment backlog

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""Validate the Economics Architect pack and spawn template.

The template is a thinking overlay for economics Sol managers. It cannot be
spawned as the master persona, a Luna worker, or a default for every manager.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
import json
import sys
from pathlib import Path
from typing import Any


ROOT = Path(__file__).resolve().parents[1]
SCHEMA = "company-os.economics-architect-spawn-template.v1"
TEMPLATE_ID = "economics-architect"
REQUIRED_SKILLS = ("manage-company-program", "economics-architect")
FORBIDDEN_ROLES = ("master", "worker")
USE_WHEN = (
    "market_sizing",
    "market_structure",
    "opportunity_cost",
    "pricing",
    "unit_economics",
)
SOURCE_FILES = (
    "00-index.txt",
    "01-resources-opportunity-cost.txt",
    "02-consumer-utility-demand.txt",
    "03-production-costs-unit-econ.txt",
    "04-supply-demand-elasticity-pricing.txt",
    "05-markets-advantage-tam-sam-som.txt",
    "06-asymmetric-information-lemons.txt",
    "07-externalities-ecosystems.txt",
    "08-macro-indicators-business-cycle.txt",
    "09-ad-as-policy-scenarios.txt",
    "10-implementation-playbook.txt",
)
TOP_LEVEL = {
    "schema",
    "template_id",
    "role",
    "requested_model",
    "skills",
    "forbidden_roles",
    "source_pack",
    "authority",
    "use_when",
}
SKILL_MARKERS = (
    "economics sol managers",
    "do not send this skill to luna workers",
    "do not use it as the master persona",
    "does not own",
    "opportunity cost",
    "do not invent tam",
)


def validate_pack(root: Path = ROOT) -> list[str]:
    errors: list[str] = []
    skill = root / "SKILL.md"
    if not skill.is_file():
        return ["missing SKILL.md"]
    text = skill.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
    if not text.startswith("---\nname: economics-architect\n"):
        errors.append("SKILL.md name must be economics-architect")
    words = len(text.split())
    if words > 700:
        errors.append(f"SKILL.md exceeds 700 words: {words}")
    folded = text.casefold()
    for marker in SKILL_MARKERS:
        if marker not in folded:
            errors.append(f"SKILL.md missing required marker: {marker}")
    if "TODO" in text:
        errors.append("SKILL.md has unresolved TODO")

    source_root = root / "references" / "source"
    for name in SOURCE_FILES:
        path = source_root / name
        if not path.is_file() or path.stat().st_size <= 0:
            errors.append(f"missing source file: {name}")
    extra = sorted(
        path.name
        for path in source_root.iterdir()
        if path.is_file() and path.name not in SOURCE_FILES
    )
    if extra:
        errors.append(f"unexpected source files: {', '.join(extra)}")

    for host in ("openai.yaml", "grok.yaml"):
        host_path = root / "agents" / host
        if not host_path.is_file():
            errors.append(f"missing agents/{host}")
            continue
        host_text = host_path.read_text(encoding="utf-8")
        if "$economics-architect" not in host_text:
            errors.append(f"agents/{host} must invoke the skill")
        if "allow_implicit_invocation: false" not in host_text:
            errors.append(f"agents/{host} must disable implicit invocation")

    template_path = root / "assets" / "spawn-template.json"
    if not template_path.is_file():
        errors.append("missing spawn template")
    else:
        try:
            payload = json.loads(template_path.read_text(encoding="utf-8"))
        except (OSError, UnicodeError, json.JSONDecodeError):
            errors.append("spawn template is unreadable JSON")
        else:
            errors.extend(validate_spawn_template(payload))
    return errors


def validate_spawn_template(payload: Any) -> list[str]:
    errors: list[str] = []
    if not isinstance(payload, dict):
        return ["spawn template must be an object"]
    extra = sorted(set(payload) - TOP_LEVEL)
    missing = sorted(TOP_LEVEL - set(payload))
    if extra:
        errors.append(f"unknown spawn keys: {', '.join(extra)}")
    if missing:
        errors.append(f"missing spawn keys: {', '.join(missing)}")
    if payload.get("schema") != SCHEMA:
        errors.append(f"schema must be {SCHEMA}")
    if payload.get("template_id") != TEMPLATE_ID:
        errors.append("template_id drifted")
    if payload.get("role") != "manager":
        errors.append("spawn role must be manager")
    if payload.get("requested_model") != "gpt-5.6-sol":
        errors.append("requested_model must remain gpt-5.6-sol")
    if payload.get("authority") != "thinking_overlay":
        errors.append("authority must be thinking_overlay")
    if payload.get("source_pack") != "references/source":
        errors.append("source_pack drifted")
    skills = payload.get("skills")
    if not isinstance(skills, list) or list(skills) != list(REQUIRED_SKILLS):
        errors.append("spawn skills must be the manager role skill plus economics-architect")
    forbidden = payload.get("forbidden_roles")
    if not isinstance(forbidden, list) or set(forbidden) != set(FORBIDDEN_ROLES):
        errors.append("forbidden_roles must be master and worker")
    use_when = payload.get("use_when")
    if not isinstance(use_when, list) or list(use_when) != list(USE_WHEN):
        errors.append("use_when must be the economics-system lanes")
    return errors


def main() -> int:
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description=__doc__)
    parser.add_argument("--root", type=Path, default=ROOT)
    args = parser.parse_args()
    errors = validate_pack(args.root)
    print(json.dumps({"valid": not errors, "errors": errors}, indent=2))
    return 0 if not errors else 1


if __name__ == "__main__":
    sys.exit(main())
